title: Profitable strategies ARE possible: 15 systematic Nasdaq strategies, 15 years of backtests, every one of them made money. Here’s the process (and what failed)
author: JayTheFknSavage
selftext:
I see a lot of posts saying nobody has a real edge, or that anyone with one would never share it. I won’t share the rules. That’s a lot of work. But I’ll share the results and the process, because the process is what actually gives people a shot.

**The scorecard**

Nasdaq futures, 5-minute chart, November 2011 to November 2026, 1 micro contract per trade, commission and slippage included. *All figures are normalized to today’s NQ contract value, so older years are comparable to recent ones.* Ranked by Sharpe ratio.

|\#|Strategy|Trades|Net P/L|PF|Win %|Max DD|Sharpe|Sortino|$/trade 2011–18|$/trade 2019–26|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|1|SAMURAI|836|$22,292|1.54|49.4%|−$1,914|1.15|2.32|\+$21.4|\+$31.2|
|2|BOUNTY HUNTER|234|$20,907|2.22|55.1%|−$2,102|1.05|2.49|\+$38.6|\+$121.6|
|3|JAILBREAK|318|$12,669|1.97|53.5%|−$1,016|1.02|2.46|\+$37.1|\+$42.8|
|4|NINJA|607|$26,414|1.56|62.4%|−$2,913|1.01|1.66|\+$24.3|\+$60.5|
|5|GHOST|588|$23,396|1.58|54.4%|−$3,323|0.98|1.84|\+$23.9|\+$53.4|
|6|SNIPER|622|$17,279|1.58|57.6%|−$1,871|0.98|1.75|\+$20.4|\+$35.5|
|7|SCYTHE|2,861|$30,582|1.18|46.5%|−$2,582|0.95|1.61|\+$9.1|\+$11.2|
|8|MERCENARY|1,100|$36,446|1.45|49.7%|−$3,699|0.95|1.95|\+$11.8|\+$52.4|
|9|GUNSLINGER|152|$9,181|2.13|58.6%|−$1,672|0.82|1.80|\+$22.8|\+$94.2|
|10|FALCON|71|$4,251|3.33|59.2%|−$388|0.76|2.38|\+$55.0|\+$61.5|
|11|HITMAN|1,715|$30,444|1.22|40.6%|−$3,812|0.75|1.54|−$1.3|\+$35.5|
|12|BLOOD HOUND|313|$19,326|1.58|53.7%|−$2,256|0.73|1.43|\+$9.7|\+$76.2|
|13|ASSASSIN|1,664|$29,895|1.28|42.1%|−$4,886|0.72|1.53|−$2.3|\+$36.9|
|14|SPEAR|766|$16,320|1.21|44.4%|−$5,348|0.49|0.90|−$8.8|\+$48.4|
|15|SCORPION|68|$6,170|1.76|57.4%|−$1,949|0.36|0.60|−$0.3|\+$206.1|
||**ALL 15 TOGETHER**|**11,915**|**$305,572**|**1.37**|**48.0%**|**−$7,390**|**1.89**|**4.48**|**+$9.6**|**+$36.9**|

**What the table actually says**

* **All 15 made money over 15 years.** There used to be a 16th. It earned less than an average trade and made the whole system slightly worse, so I tested it and cut it. That’s how it should work: strategies earn their spot, and nothing stays because I like it.
* **No single strategy is a holy grail.** The best Sharpe on its own is 1.15. HITMAN wins only 41% of the time and still nets $30K, because its winners are bigger than its losers. Win rate is overrated. PF and drawdown tell you much more.
* **Combining them is the real edge.** Together the Sharpe jumps to 1.89, and the worst drawdown across all 15 is about −$7,400 on $305K of profit. They don’t all lose at the same time, so their bad stretches partly cancel out.
* **Markets change, and the table shows it.** 11 of 15 made money in *both* eras. Four (HITMAN, ASSASSIN, SPEAR, SCORPION) earned close to nothing in the calm 2011–18 market and carried their weight from 2019 on. That’s why I check every era separately and don’t just trust the total.

**How I got here: the part nobody can hand you**

1. **I write the pass/fail rule BEFORE seeing any results, every time.** Look at results first and you’ll always find a way to make them look good.
2. **Every strategy has to beat a random-entry control:** same number of trades, random entry times, same exits. If a signal can’t beat random, it’s not a signal. This step alone killed most of my ideas.
3. **Every strategy is checked in different market eras.** One great era isn’t enough.
4. **Costs are in everything:** commission and slippage.
5. **Most ideas failed. A lot of them.** Popular indicators, filters, exits I was sure about, trailing stops, influencer setups. Well over 100 tests, and the large majority came back FAIL. The 15 above are what survived. The failures are why I trust the survivors.

**Where it stands now**

It runs automatically and is being forward-tested live, with a weekly review comparing live results to what the backtest expected. The “off track” line was written down in advance: if live goes past the worst drawdown or the longest losing streak the backtest ever showed, it gets pulled for review, not re-optimized.

A backtest is a hypothesis, not a promise. The forward record decides. I’ll update as it builds.

**The point**

If you’re grinding and nothing works yet: that’s normal. Edges exist. You don’t find them by asking for someone’s setup. You find them by testing honestly, letting most of your ideas die, and keeping what survives. Write your rules first, test against random, test across different markets, and include costs.

Happy to answer questions about the process.

comments.author: koryuken
comments.body: Now map that to just holding nasdaq for same time frame and give us delta. I'm going to guess delta is small or zero?

replies.author: JayTheFknSavage
replies.body:
Fair question, so I ran it. Same 15 years, same scoring (normalized to today’s NQ value), 1 micro:

||15 strategies|Buy and hold 1 MNQ|
|:-|:-|:-|
|Net|$306K|$153K|
|Sharpe|1.73|0.83|
|Max drawdown|−$7.3K|−$21.3K|
|Correlation to Nasdaq|0.08|1.00|

So not zero: roughly 2× the profit with about a third of the drawdown, and it’s nearly uncorrelated with the index, so it isn’t just long beta. To be fair, buy-and-hold actually won 2011–18 ($62.6K vs $47.5K). The system’s edge came mostly from 2019 on. The bigger win is the risk side: a 15-year worst drawdown of $7.3K vs $21.3K.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the 2011-18 vs 2019-26 split is the column I'd stare at. nearly all 15 earn more per trade in the second half, a few of them 3-4x, even after you normalized to today's contract. that's either a regime the rules happen to like or a sign they were shaped on recent data. how many candidates did you test to end up with these 15?

replies.author: JayTheFknSavage
replies.body:
I'm glad I found someone who would notice. Good catch, and it’s the right column to stare at. Honest answer: it’s some of both.

Part is regime. NQ’s average daily range was about 1.14% of price in 2011–18 vs 1.55% in 2019–26, roughly 36% bigger moves now. Normalizing to today’s contract doesn’t remove that, and trend-following rules earn more per trade when the market moves more.

But that doesn’t explain 3–4× on a few of them, and I won’t pretend it does. Most of these were designed while looking at 2019–26 data (MNQ only exists from 2019), so 2011–18 is a partial out-of-sample check, not a clean one. The few that are weakest in 2011–18 are the ones I trust least.

On candidates: roughly 100+ hand-built ideas tested one at a time, each with its pass rule written first and a random-entry control. I also ran automated searches over millions of rule combinations, and those found zero survivors after holdout and random checks. The 15 are what’s left from the hand-built side. Where I’ve tested many variants, I use a deflated Sharpe to account for it.

Which is why the real test is the forward record. It’s running live now, and I’ll post how it compares to these numbers.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: a 36% wider daily range covers some of it, just not a 3-4x jump per trade on its own. the rest is where the candidate count would tell you which story you're in.

replies.author: JayTheFknSavage
replies.body: I agree. With \~100 hand-built candidates behind the 15, some of that 3–4× is very likely selection, rules shaped by what worked recently, not just a wider range. I haven’t deflated the 15 as a set against the full candidate count yet, only the individual searches. That’s the next check I’ll run. Until then, I’d treat the 2011–18 column as the more honest estimate of what the rules are really worth, and the 2019–26 numbers as optimistic. The forward record will settle which story it is.

replies.author: JayTheFknSavage
replies.body:
Ran it. Counting honestly: \~124 ideas with logged results, \~400 written test plans, plus automated searches (hundreds of thousands of strategies, none survived holdout). The 15 came from the hand-built pool.

You’re right about the eras. Four of the 15 lost or broke even in 2011–18, and combined it’s Sharpe 1.0 in 2011–18 vs 2.4 in 2019–26.

Bailey / López de Prado deflated Sharpe: individually, none of the 15 clears 95% once you count the candidates. The combined book sits at 0.95 at N≈400 (0.995 at 124, \~0.55 if you count the automated searches conservatively). So I’m treating it as a positive-in-both-eras system whose recent results are probably optimistic, and the forward record is what decides. Curious how you’d count N for automated searches.

replies.author: JayTheFknSavage
replies.body:
Ran the numbers you were asking for.

**Candidate count:** \~124 ideas with logged results, \~400 written test plans, plus automated searches (hundreds of thousands of strategies, zero survived holdout). The 15 came from the hand-built pool.

**You were right about the eras.** Combined Sharpe is 1.0 in 2011–18 vs 2.4 in 2019–26, and four of the 15 lost or broke even in the first half.

**Deflated Sharpe (Bailey / López de Prado):** individually, none of the 15 clears 95% once you count the candidates. The combined book is 0.948 at N≈400 (0.995 at 124, \~0.55 if you count the automated searches conservatively). So the backtest alone isn’t proof, and I’d treat the 2011–18 numbers as the honest estimate.

**What the forward record says so far** (rules frozen Nov 3, live data, 1 micro):Caveat: one big trend day (+$7K) carries it. Since then it’s slightly red. 168 trades doesn’t settle anything, so I’ll keep posting it good or bad.

|Metric|Live|Backtest|
|:-|:-|:-|
|Trades|168|11,915|
|$ per trade|\+$35.9|\~+$26|
|Profit factor|1.61|1.37|
|Worst drawdown|$2,152|$7,390|

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: 1.0 then 2.4, with four of the 15 flat or red in the first half, is a straight answer, thanks for running it. I'd size off the 1.0 until the set-level deflation is done and treat the rest as unearned for now.

replies.author: JayTheFknSavage
replies.body:
**My table broke in that reply, I edited it.**  
The labels ended up under “Live”, the live numbers sit under “Backtest”, and the backtest column disappeared.  
  
Also I agree, and that’s how I’m treating it: sizing off the 2011–18 numbers, and the 2019–26 half stays unearned until the forward record backs it up. Thanks for pushing on it. This thread made the system better. But any idea why the mods might have removed it?

comments.author: oonlineoonly2
comments.body: Where can I find all these strategy details?

replies.author: JayTheFknSavage
replies.body: They’re my own and I’m not sharing the rules, sorry. That’s months of testing and long sleepless nights. What I’m happy to share is the process, since that’s what gets you to your own: write the pass/fail rule before you test, make every idea beat random entries, check it in different market eras, and include costs. Most ideas will fail, and that’s normal. The ones that survive are yours, and you’ll understand them far better than anything copied.
